Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture.
As a result of a statement made recently by the Minister of Agriculture regarding the Agricultural Stabilization Act, there is some confusion among milk producers. Here is my question: If a producer ships milk or cream to a retailer in Montreal or in any other city, is he eligible for a deficiency payment? If not, why should he keep shipping his milk to that retailer if he can get a deficiency payment of 25 cents per hundred pounds by sending it to a milk powder, butter or cheese manufacturer?
(Text):

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PAYMENTS ON SHIPMENTS TO MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with there is
no such thing as a deficiency payment as far as milk is concerned. There is a payment, a flat payment which is not a deficiency payment, of 25 cents per 100 pounds of whole milk delivered for manufacturing purposes.
The situation essentially is this. A man who is delivering cream for butter making is in exactly the same position as he was during the year previous to May 1 of this year, and should be receiving exactly the same price. The milk producer who is delivering fluid milk for consumption and who is thus receiving the fluid milk price, which runs from 75 to 100 per cent more than the price for manufacturing milk, is not eligible to receive the 25 cents per 100 pounds payment. Producers who deliver their milk for manufacturing purposes are eligible, however, for this payment of 25 cents per 100 pounds of whole milk delivered.

He has already had to pay an interest rate of 4.49 per cent on his initial issue, so what kind of interest rate may he well have to offer before March 31 next?
The minister also went to great length to explain the difference between rates on issues for which he is responsible and on the offerings of the United States government. He indicated yesterday that an offering almost like the one that he put out yesterday, a one-year United States treasury bill, produced a yield of 4.05 per cent. I assume that is in terms of United States dollars which means that in terms of Canadian dollars the yield would be slightly under 4 per cent. However, the money invested is United States money so it would be 4.05 per cent. For years now our dollar has been worth more than the United States dollar and we fail to understand why an offering by the Canadian Minister of Finance should have to pay an effective rate of 4.49 per cent when south of the border, where their money is worth less, they are able to obtain money for 4.05 per cent.
The minister was very mixed up in his interpretation of the billion dollars that has to leave Canada to pay homage to United States investment in Canada. It had nothing whatever to do with the fact that our dollar is worth more than the United States dollar. I simply reminded the minister of the information that has been available on the financial pages of the newspapers for several months that out of the 1958 Canadian economy there had to be paid to United States investors in Canada, by way of earnings on United
Interim Supply
States investment in Canada, by way of interest rates on United States holdings of Canadian securities, a sum of money in excess of a billion dollars. The minister, himself, by listing United States investments in Canada tended to confirm these newspaper reports. He indicated that there was invested in Canada by United States investors a sum of money in excess of $18,000 million, and the return on that is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 4.5 per cent. I am not saying the return is excessive at all.
However, I am attempting to point out that the failure of the government of Canada to supply leadership to the Canadian people, to supply the incentive to the Canadian people to be responsible for the development of Canadian enterprise, the failure of their leadership to appeal to the patriotism of the Canadian people to have confidence in the Canada of tomorrow, leads us to rely more and more for our prosperity on the confidence and faith that others have in us and in our resources. This places us ever more in hock to outside interests. The longer this condition is permitted to continue, the longer we are postponing the event. Some day Shylock will demand his pound of flesh and the Canadian people will suffer the consequence. I know that this is not peculiar to the federal Minister of Finance. Almost all levels of government and very certainly most individual Canadians are living beyond their means. However, hitherto the federal ministers of finance have been the prime leaders in sponsoring the philosophy that we can continue to borrow to keep pace with eternal prosperity. Those days must end, and they will end.
The sooner that Canadians in all walks of life, under the leadership of the Minister of Finance, begin to realize that we have to buy for the growing boy a new set of breeches every year, that if necessary we have to reduce our expenditures in order that we might eventually own Canada ourselves, the better off we will be. However, the minister continues to place blind reliance on the money market, puts his head in the sand and hopes that maybe tomorrow the sun will shine. He compares himself with the minister of finance of Saskatchewan. There simply is no comparison between the authority and power of this federal Minister of Finance and the authority and power of the minister of finance of any province. I believe even the minister will agree that compared to other provinces, the minister of finance of Saskatchewan, Mr. Fines, has done well indeed.
The minister asks, what is our remedy? He offers what he imagines is our remedy. He says, by implication at least, that the
C.C.F. is advocating we use the printing press.
I believe the Minister of Finance knows', 'Interim Supply
better than that. Throughout its entire history, while the C.C.F. has advocated monetary reform, it has never advocated turning the handle of the printing press and turning out money for which there is no value. There is only one political movement of which I know that has advocated that, and that is the Social Credit movement. Let me warn the minister that if he pursues his present course of action, those irresponsible advocates of monetary reform are going to grow in influence throughout Canada. I am very annoyed, and I regret very much the evidence of the growth of a movement such as the Union des Electeurs in Quebec, where they are able to persuade municipality after municipality that the minister should use the Bank of Canada to finance, without interest, all the capital needs of our municipal governments. The list of municipalities advocating this measure is becoming alarmingly large.
This is an irresponsible recommendation and the minister well knows it is irresponsible. However, if the minister is going to follow his reactionary policies these counter movements are going to grow. You will find one city council after another throughout Canada endorsing the submissions of the Union des Electeurs. We have never advocated the issuance of more currency than is necessary to meet the needs of the Canadian economy. However, we have asked the minister to make a survey by means of a national investment board, royal commission or otherwise-let him decide whatever means he thinks best- of the credit resources available within the Canadian economy. We have asked for a survey of the credit needs of the various levels of government in Canada, of industrial enterprises and of individuals in Canada. The minister has, hitherto, laughed off all these recommendations.
I should like to spend many minutes more in offering many other recommendations as to how the minister might undertake measures that would relieve him of the very difficult situation in which I think he ought to admit he is. Our submission is that the sooner the minister admits he is in difficulty, the sooner we will begin to find a solution and, as real Canadians we will work our way out of the predicament in which we are now.
Resolution reported and concurred in.']

The committee will recall that one previous vote of interim supply has been made in respect to the present fiscal year in the amount of $616,654,878.69, to provide for the expenses of government for the first two months of the fiscal year. The proportion of nearly all the items voted on that occasion was, accordingly, one-sixth. There were, however, 12 items of a rather special nature for which additional proportions were then voted.
In the present resolution the committee is asked to vote an additional one-sixth of all items, both in the main estimates and the supplementary estimates, plus additional fractions in respect of 20 items. These 20 items are, of course, of a special or seasonal nature in so far as the programs to which they relate are affected. As to those 20 items, the additional proportions vary according to the nature of the program. The maximum which will be voted, if this present resolution carries, will, in the case of no item, exceed eleven-twelfths, and there are only two items in respect of which the vote proposed today will bring the proportion appropriated to that
Interim Supply
fraction of eleven-twelfths. They are items 66 and 102. The committee accordingly retains its full right to discuss and debate all items in the estimates.
I give also, Mr. Chairman, the time-honoured undertaking that the passage of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure. That undertaking, Mr. Chairman, is given, if I may remind the committee, for the purpose of avoiding duplication of debate. What is expressly acknowledged in this way protects the rights of hon. members to discuss every item when it comes up in due course in committee of supply.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Minister of Finance and the committee, too, will be gratified to hear me say that my remarks will be brief. As far as I know, although each individual member has considerable rights under this particular resolution the official opposition, certainly through me, is not launching any major debate at this stage. We recognize that while three departments of the government have already passed through the committee of supply, it happens that in the supplementary estimates there are items with respect to each of those departments and very shortly we shall be discussing all the other departments in committee of supply. Therefore, as I say, we are not taking advantage of this motion to launch a debate which might be in the nature of a duplication. We want to facilitate the processes of the house in that way.
As the minister has stated, Mr. Chairman, there are one or two items that provide for more than four-twelfths of the appropriation in the book of estimates. There are just one or two on which I should like a little more information. I was wondering about item 66. As the minister has stated, we are here providing eleven-twelfths of the year's appropriation for the item with respect to additional service to the Indians of British Columbia. I wondered whether the minister would just put on the record a little more information in that respect. Then I would be a little curious about item 358. It is the public works item, general. The reason is that it seems early in the season to be asking for more than a normal advance on this item because it is entitled, "Balances re building projects undertaken in previous fiscal years for which no specific provision is made in

Interim Supply
fiscal year 1959-60." I wonder whether the minister would just give us the detail on this item.
While we are getting reminders oi the items that we have to make appropriation for in stages, I think none the less all of us recognize that even these fractions are for very considerable sums. We see now why the supplementary estimates were introduced the other day. It makes it possible for the minister also to obtain one-sixth of each of the items in the $120 million of supple-mentaries. But when we compare the first supplementaries of this year with those of last year, we are comparing $120 million with $58 million. This means an increase of $62 million in the first stage of the supplementaries, and we all know that when we compare the main estimates of this year with those of last year they show an increase of $416 million. Therefore when we take these two first stages of appropriations through the estimates we can see that as of this short period of time in the new year we have an increase of $478 million in over-all expenditures.

Mr. Chairman, I realize it is usual to have a rather limited debate take place at the resolution stage having to do with interim supply. However, we are unable to ignore the fact that the minister is asking for a little in excess of half a billion dollars to be voted.
We have a matter which in our opinion is rather urgent at this time. For years now it has been the habit of the house to delay the estimates of the Minister of Finance until very near the end of the session. Since the interim supply bill has to do at least in a measure with the estimates of the Minister of Finance, including the estimate providing for the administrative expenses of the department he heads, I feel that I have to raise a matter that we consider of urgent national public importance at this time. It has to do with the policies now being pursued by the minister in regard to the management of the debt of the government of Canada.
I would like immediately to express our understanding of and our sympathy with the problems of the minister. This year he has to raise on the money markets on behalf of the government of Canada by way of loans an amount in excess of $2,000 million. This is a very large amount for any year excepting a year of war. We realize what are the minister's responsibilities. In the first place, he has to get the people of Canada or elsewhere to express enough confidence in the government to lend him another $2,000 million in this one year. He also has to assure the

Canadian economy that its credit needs are going to be met. He has to assure that out of the available investment money, in addition to the $2,000 million that he himself needs, enough will be left over to meet the needs of Canadian enterprise and of provincial and municipal governments as well as of individuals who need credit.
We also realize that, apart from the minister's responsibility, in addition to getting in excess of $2,000 million for the federal government, and in addition to assuring that all the other credit needs of Canada, municipal, provincial, industrial and personal will be met, the overriding desire of the minister is to restore and maintain public confidence in our monetary system.
I could use various terms or forms of language in making my appeal to the minister.
I could appeal to him in the language of one ex-Sunday school superintendent to another ex-Sunday school superintendent. However, I realize immediately that the minister would say that what we say on Sunday does not necessarily hold on a cold and frosty Monday morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never said that.

I might use the language of the Marxists and attempt to educate the minister as to some of the teachings of Karl Marx. However, I realize that would not be of very much value in this house under present conditions. Therefore I shall do my utmost to express our opinions in the minister's own language. I hope it will not be the language of Bay street or St. James street but the language of ordinary, patriotic Canadians. I should like to say that we have abiding confidence in the ultimate wisdom of the electorate of Canada.
I should like to refer to an announcement the minister made last night respecting the result of the bids on his latest treasury bill offering. Yesterday the minister announced that he had been able to borrow $200 million. That is less than 10 per cent of the amount he will have to borrow in the current fiscal year. He announced that the price obtained for one year treasury bills was $94.78 per $100, which produces a yield to those who invested of 5.492 per cent. In other words the Minister of Finance admitted that in order to borrow $200 million for the government of Canada for a period of one year he had to pay an effective interest rate of 54 per cent, or very nearly that, on a one-year federal government issue.
I know the minister likes to sugar coat the pill, and he has used a number of devices. He called this an issue of treasury bills

when in fact it was an issue of bonds. To all intents and purposes and for all practical purposes it is a one year government bond. However, I suppose the minister, acting on behalf of the people of Canada, had the idea that he might get a better rate by calling it a treasury bill rather than a bond.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The two things are quite different.

He admitted that it was something new in Canadian government financial history to issue a treasury bill with a duration of 365 days when treasury bills are usually of 90 days' duration. The minister admitted further weakness in his position when he indicated that those who converted the 2J per cent 1959 bonds for the new treasury bills would be able to collect on June 10 the payment falling due at the end of that month. In other words a 20-day bonus was given to the holders of the 2J per cent 1959 bonds.
The minister also announced last night, in response to a question by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, that this treasury bill issue was one that might be used by the banks of Canada for deposit as a reserve with the Bank of Canada. Thereby the minister admitted that the issuance of these treasury bills was highly inflationary, in that an issue was being made that might be used for purposes of reserve with the Bank of Canada, replacing in effect a bond issue that was not acceptable for reserve purposes by the Bank of Canada.
Our complaint is that the minister is facing increasing difficulties and that in the light of that situation he is doing nothing about it. He is burying his head in the sand and, as far as we know, the government is not contemplating any action to head off the crisis that is approaching. The government seems to think that by a little bit of sugar coating, such as making bonds acceptable at par on June 10 when they should only be acceptable on June 30; such as making the new bonds acceptable by the Bank of Canada for reserve purposes, replacing bonds that were not acceptable; such as calling a bond a treasury bill rather than a bond, and by hiding our heads in the sand we may be able to avoid the growing crisis in the matter of government financing. The government, as far as we now know, is placing its undying faith in the money market place and hoping that events and circumstances will rescue it from the dilemma in which it now is.
I read in the newspaper this morning that at North Bay last night the Prime Minister had recited a number of instances that to him were signs of the return of prosperity to the Canadian economy. I know the Prime Minister is equally aware that he might also
Interim Supply
have used all kinds of figures, facts and statistics to prove exactly the opposite of the main tenor of his remarks last night. On a number of occasions we have asked the government to produce evidence of the return of prosperity to the Canadian economic scene, and we have received very vague replies indeed. For every instance of a return to a growing prosperity that the government is able to report, the opposition is equally able to record other enterprises in Canada that are on the downgrade at the present time.
One of the main evidences of a return to economic prosperity put forward by the minister over the past several months has been the demand being made at the present time on the resources of the banks. The remarks of the minister have had a strange uniformity. A number of us are asking ourselves, who is making all these demands on the banks now? Is it possibly the government itself which is absorbing all the available resources of the banks at the present time, or is there really a grass roots expansion of the economy and are Canadian enterprises really asking for additional loans from the banks with which to expand?
When I look at the rate of interest the minister announced last night I can appreciate that the banks might not be very interested in making any loans to Canadian industrial enterprises, that the banks might not be very interested in helping the Canadian economy expand. After all, if banks are able to make their resources available to the Minister of Finance and obtain a rate of interest of 5.5 per cent, why should the banks be interested in any way, shape or form in making their money available to Canadian enterprises at the maximum rate of 6 per cent?
I am referring now particularly to a fear that is rather widespread that the government of the day may very soon be seeking the authorization of parliament to amend the Bank Act. I have in my hand a copy of the Toronto Telegram for the day before yesterday, and the headline on the business and financial page is "Would boost rate on Bank and N.H.A. loans". I know the minister will agree with me that if he has to pay 5.5 per cent on one year treasury bills, he cannot possibly very long delay permission to the banks of Canada to raise the maximum allowable interest rate. He cannot very long delay the day when the maximum interest rate will be raised under the National Housing Act. He cannot very long delay the day when the maximum interest rate allowable under the Canadian farm loan board, as well as many other enterprises, will have to be raised. He cannot delay the day much longer, unless

Interim Supply
he changes his approach to the basic problem of public financing, when he will have to raise interest rates for all the major segments of the Canadian economy.
I realize that the Minister of Finance is possibly the most important man in the government, Mr. Chairman. I realize that the government must have a front, a showman at the head of it. However, over the years it has been hammered home to the Canadian electorate that the real man guiding the destinies of all of us is the federal Minister of Finance. Why our Prime Minister decided to select one of the most orthodox, one of the most faithful of men, who subscribes to the outmoded and discredited economic and financial policies, as Minister of Finance is beyond me. We have seen how month after month the tension has been mounting. We know our Prime Minister is a progressive. We know he is a westerner. We know he is willing to experiment, that he is willing to explore the unknown. We know, Mr. Chairman, that he was even able to take the remains of a completely dead Conservative movement and catapult it into office. However, why he ever decided to select as the most important minister in the government a man who is dedicated to pursuing outmoded and outworn economic policies is beyond our comprehension.
He should have got you; you are the smart guy.
I know the minister is willing to concede-
You are from B.C., a real wizard.

-that if we are going to relieve unemployment in Canada, if we are going to maintain economic prosperity, our economy has to grow. There is no such thing as standing still. Our economy must expand. I also know that if we are going to follow a policy of aiding production we will have to develop markets, and in this day and age the development of markets is going to cost us money. The other day the Prime Minister announced that there was $10 million available for flour here and so many million dollars available for milk products there. The development of markets to meet growing production is going to mean more money from the federal government.
Hitherto we have relied on investors in the United States for the expansion of our economy, with the result that our dollar is worth more than the United States dollar. This is imposing a hardship on all our exporters, and it is also imposing a hardship on Canadian manufacturing enterprises. Our reliance on the United States is going to

cost us a great deal in the years ahead. Indeed, it has already proven very expensive in so far as earnings are concerned in the form of dividends, profits and interest. The interest on what we owed south of the border last year took over a billion dollars away from Canadian production. I know the minister realizes that the all expansion of the Canadian economy has to come from the production of Canadian workers, out of unused production here, out of the savings of the people of our own land. We should like at this time to appeal to the minister for a little bit of leadership in order that we might eventually be masters of our own destiny.
Our proposal in this regard is that the minister, in the first place, should admit that he is in serious difficulty.
I should like to see him make a confession to the people of Canada. We realize that he alone is not responsible. Other governments and other ministers before his day have also added to the situation. Rather than to make a gamble or a play with the future welfare of the Canadian economy and the lives of our Canadian workers we should like to see him make a confession and the confession would say in effect that our riches have not expanded with the growth of the country. Our Canadian economy has expanded but, unlike the wise parent, we have failed to supply the boy with a new pair of britches annually and now in many parts of his anatomy the young lad is exposed and is at the mercy of others. Advantage is now being taken of our predicament.
I am sure that no Conservative regime in other areas of the British commonwealth would place such faith in the money market as our minister is doing. The investors of Canada are not misled. They are men who know what they are doing. They know that they have the minister over a barrel, and they know that they can extract even more blood than they are obtaining right now. That is why the minister yesterday was obliged to pay almost 5J per cent on a one-year issue of the federal government. I had a phone call out of the municipality of Coquitlam over the noon hour and learned that they were able to issue 20-year bonds and all they have to pay is an effective rate of 6.3 per cent. I asked the municipal clerk what was the reason for that. He said that after the let-down which the people of Canada have experienced at the hands of the federal government over the years, you cannot blame the investors of Canada for having almost as much faith-in effect it is a greater expression of a faith-in the issue of

a municipal government as they have in an issue being placed on the market by the Minister of Finance.
Anyone who knows anything about the investment field at all knows that a 6.3 per cent rate on a 20-year issue is in effect a lower rate than a 5.49 per cent rate on a one-year issue that has the backing of the federal government. We have therefore now arrived at the stage where the investors of Canada are expressing greater confidence and faith in our municipal governments and in our provincial governments than they are expressing in our present Minister of Finance.
We say that the investors are not misled. We say that the people are lacking in faith in the government of the day. We say that it is high time that there be an assessment of the credit needs of the Canadian nation, the federal government, all other levels of government, all levels of Canadian enterprise and of individuals. We should like at this time to ask the Minister of Finance this question. He has now financed a tenth of his needs for this year. What plans has he in mind to meet his needs for the rest of the year? How in the world is he going to be able to borrow $1,800 million more or less at an adequate rate of interest?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take very many minutes of the time of the committee but I want to refer to interest rates. On Monday when questions were being asked the Minister of Finance regarding the current treasury bill rate, as reported at page 4192 of Hansard I asked him this question:
Is the minister aware that the highest United States short term treasury bill rate is 3 per cent, while our own exceeds 5 per cent, a differential of over 2 per cent?
Then the minister replied as follows:
With respect, Mr. Speaker, a very misleading impression has been left by the observation which the hon. gentleman has just made, and I would ask the opportunity to set that right. Evidently the hon. member is not aware of the situation with respect to treasury bill rates in the United States. I happen to have them with me in a statement which reached my desk only today. On the 340 day bills in the United States the rate is 3.835 per cent average: on the 220 day bills it is 3.565 per cent average, and on the 1 year certificates, the 4 per cent coupon is offered on a 4.05 per cent basis.
The minister is right except that he has assumed his old trick of comparing apples with oranges, as he did when he tabled the estimates for this year. He compared this year's estimates with last year's estimates plus the supplementary estimates plus supplementary estimates No. 1 and supplementary estimates No. 2. When I asked him the question my reference was to the 91 day treasury bills and not to the treasury bills for six months, 220 66968-9-273
Interim Supply
days or over seven months or to those running one year or slightly under one year.
Short term treasury bills.

For treasury bills those are considered to be long term. In the financial papers on Saturday-I do not want to read them but I have them here-it is stated that Canada had to pay 5J per cent for 91 day loans while the United States government needs to pay only 3 per cent for 91 day or short term borrowings in treasury bills, and that in the United States it is expected that the supply of short term money will increase this year, thus forcing down interest rates in that country.
I learned from the Bank of Canada that Canada had sold six months treasury bills to yield 5.26 per cent. In comparing the last sales of 91 day treasury bills in the United States and ours I find that Canada on May 22 sold treasury bills to yield 5.05 per cent and that the United States on May 25-three days later-sold treasury bills that yielded 2.88 per cent, which showed a differential of 2.17 per cent.
I realize that last week-and I have heard it since-the Bank of Canada obtained a more favourable rate than the 5.05 per cent, that the rate had gone down to slightly under 5 per cent and that in the United States it went up slightly. Therefore that differential could be decreased. But I was certainly surprised to hear the minister announce with some pride last night that this treasury bill loan was over subscribed. I wondered why it would not be over subscribed with such a high rate of interest of almost 5J per cent. I was wondering if this would augur well for our provinces, our municipalities, our school boards and business organizations generally having to borrow money here in Canada. They will certainly have to pay a much higher interest rate.
In the financial press last Saturday I saw two or three references to the banks crediting the terrific spread between interest rates in Canada and those in the United States to the ballooning of the Canadian dollar premium. One report said that more money was coming in from the United States to Canada for investment in projects for high interest rates, and that tends to keep up the premium. According to Mr. Ambridge of the Abitibi Power and Paper Company, this makes it very hard for primary producers to sell their products in the United States. He goes on to say that each one cent increase in the premium slashes the income of our newspaper industry alone by more than $6 million a year.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up the time of the committee, but I heard the

Interim Supply
previous speaker making reference to the amount of money which had to be raised or refinanced this year along with the amount of money which had to be raised on capital and current loans. I know that the minister told us in a three-hour speech that the government had nothing to do whatsoever with setting interest rates. I also recall that the minister came into the house on November 14, 1957 and told us that no previous government in Canada's history had accomplished as much in five months for the good of the people of Canada as this government, and I know a lot of hon. gentlemen here will agree with that. But in support of his thesis on that day he said he was happy to report that in the weekly issue of treasury bills at that date the government had achieved a reduction of at least two-tenths of 1 per cent. The Prime Minister also said on the hustings and in Calgary that the interest rates in this country had fallen sharply as the result of government action since last June. I would think that if both these gentlemen have any control over interest rates and have magic wands, now is the time to use them because interest rates are going up week after week. Talking of interest rates-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The government is not doing much about them, not even the Minister of Finance.

-the $100 million loan of the government last February cost this government an effective interest rate of 6.6 per cent. I say that the farmer and the corner grocery man can go down and borrow money from the bank at the present time at a cheaper rate than the government did on that occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked me for some further information as to the reason why an additional fraction on items 66 and 358 is now being asked. Item 66 is an item of $100,000 described in the estimates as a grant to provide additional services to the Indians of British Columbia. I may say to him that interest in this particular program, which embraces irrigation and agricultural products, is greater than ever before. It is essentially a summer program and the bulk of the funds are expected to be spent before the end of July.
As to item 358, may I remind the house that this is an item of $800,000 described in the estimates as:
Balances required to complete any projects undertaken in previous fiscal years and for which no specific provision is made in the fiscal year 1959-60.
May I point out, Mr. Chairman, that by its nature this vote is used in the early months

of each year to complete projects carried forward from the previous fiscal year.
I also noted the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River concerning the supplementary estimates. Some reference was also made to that by other speakers. I think, Mr. Chairman, that there has been some oversight here on the part of the hon. gentlemen. It is important that the basis of comparison should be clear and fair. In comparing the non-statutory items in the 1959-60 main estimates with the 1958-59 main estimates, plus supplementary estimates Nos. 1 and 2, there was in this year's estimates, as I pointed out when tabling them in February, a decrease of $39.1 million.
Let us compare main with main. As somebody said, let us compare oranges with oranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But let us talk about things which are controllable. I am talking about that when I draw the attention of the house to the relationship of fairly comparable items. In comparing the 1959-60 main estimates-
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -plus the supplementary estimates-
Take out the pluses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -which I tabled on Monday, with the 1958-59 estimates plus the supplementary estimates Nos. 1 and 2, there is an increase of $15 million in nonstatutory items. In comparing the 1959-60 main estimates plus the supplementary estimates which I tabled on Monday with the 1958-59 main estimates plus the supplementary estimates Nos. 1 and 2 and final supplementary estimates 1958-59, there is a decrease in 1959-60 of $267.8 million in the non-statutory items.
Does not the minister get confused from using so many different sets of figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. These are all plain figures which are on the record, if the hon. gentleman takes the trouble to analyse them.
To pick out the right ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now, Mr. Chairman, I will direct my observations to the remarks made by the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam. He prefaced his remarks with a statement somewhat to this effect, that he was capable of giving me some instruction in the language of Marxism. If so I must confess I have no reason to pursue him into that field. I regret to say in general

of his remarks today that I have rarely heard more unadulterated nonsense talked in the House of Commons.

The minister says that
about every speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First of all, he began with the curious statement that a treasury bill and a bond are the same thing. Mr. Chairman, everybody else in the House of Commons, I am sure, knows that while these are both Canadian government obligations, they are different in their nature. A bond is an obligation put out by the government with a coupon rate set by the government. A treasury bill is an invitation by those interested to buy at a price to be stated by them in their tender. It is an obligation on the part of the government of Canada to pay them a fixed round sum at an appointed date, whether it be at the end of three months, six months, nine months, or a year, as the case may be.
The hon. gentleman then went on to-
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is not apparent to the hon. gentleman, then all I can say, speaking in sorrow rather than anger, is that I think it is perfectly clear to everybody else in the house and that perhaps we had better proceed. The hon. gentleman seemed to take some satisfaction from what he said was the lack of faith on the part of the people of Canada with regard to these obligations issued by the government.
I did no such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I heard a great deal from him about lack of faith on the part of the Canadian people.
No satisfaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will simply take what comfort I think can properly be taken by the government and by hon. members of this house and I think by the great majority of the Canadian people from the fact that yesterday's invitation to subscribe and tender for treasury bills up to $200 million resulted, as I had pleasure in announcing in this house last night, in a very heavy over-subscription.
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It means something that evidently the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam does not understand and does not like.
I dare you to explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These are tenders on the part of persons who were prepared to indicate their confidence with regard to
66968-9-2731
Interim, Supply
obligations to be discharged by the government of Canada one year from the date of issue.
Something was said by the hon. member about the rate. Everyone knows-or, at least, everyone else knows-that these various treasury bills have rates which bear a relationship to the maturity date. We in this country have not been accustomed to having one-year treasury bills. We had nine-months treasury bills back in 1955 under the former government, but if one looks at the figures in the United States, or at the relationship in Canada between treasury bills and the various maturity dates, it will be seen that practically uniformly the effective rate, that is the discount rate, or the "equivalent yield", is higher according to the length of the maturity. In other words, the discount is lower on the 91-day bills than it is on the six-months bills, nine-months bills or 12-months bills, and having regard to the rates obtaining latterly in the market on these very short term obligations the rate on the 12-months bill on our offering of up to $200 million is in line with the rates prevailing.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, no minister of finance likes paying any more in the way of interest on the money that he must borrow than he is obliged to do. I do not intend to go back over the ground I covered on a previous occasion when I pointed out the extent to which the extraordinarily heavy demand for money today is a direct consequence of the rapidity of expansion and the forces of recovery at work in the Canadian economy which have forced interest rates to higher levels. This is not a situation confined to Canada. It is a situation which is paralleled precisely by the situation in the United States and it is reflected there in higher interest rates on all manner of securities. I have before me the rates paid on United States treasury bills-the 91-day rates. They show that the rate today is the highest prevailing during the entire period since last December. On 182-day treasury bills in the United States the rate prevailing today is the highest in this period-
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The equivalent rate is 3.489, and that is the highest rate in the period of which I am speaking, beginning last December. Our experience is not exceptional. It is precisely the experience of the United States, and for similar reasons, namely, that there is an extraordinarily heavy demand for money. Similarly, on a previous occasion in this house I discussed the results of the bidding on the 221-day treasury bills of May 15, and there the equivalent rate of discount was 3.565 per cent. Again, on May 11, on

Interim Supply
the 340-day United States treasury bills the rate was 3.835 per cent. So it is quite clear to anyone who has followed rates at all that the rates on treasury bills rise according to the length of maturity. And I have pointed out that the rate existing in the United States today on the 91-day treasury bills and the 182-day treasury bills is the highest in the past six months.
Again, let us take note of what has been happening in Canada. It is true that, as we discussed this subject a month ago in this house, the treasury bill rate was rising in Canada, and for the reasons I have mentioned-
Are there any other reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are always many reasons that operate, but we are speaking now of the effective and strong factors which are accounting for the movement of interest rates today, and while the treasury bill rate in Canada on the 91-day bills did rise in recent weeks, as we were reminded, the fact is that last week the treasury bill rate was down. The rate in the previous week was virtually the same on 91-day bills as it had been the week before that but, as I say, the rate last week was down whereas in the United States it rose. Similarly, on the 182-day bills the rate last week was down. In Canada, we have had offerings now over a period of the last four weeks on 182-day treasury bills, and the offering of May 29 sold at the lowest rate in this period. These are short periods, and I do not intend to draw any sweeping conclusions from these facts, but I think, in fairness, that when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam undertakes to speak on this subject he should speak with knowledge of the facts and not in the manner he did today.
As far as the difference between interest rates in Canada and rates in United States is concerned, let me remind the committee that there has always been a difference in these rates. All effective interest rates in Canada have always been higher than those in the United States, and for a good reason. Canada is an importer of capital; Canada, as an underdeveloped country needs capital. The United States, on the other hand, is a country with a highly developed economy and a country which has a great reservoir of capital. Take any type of security at all-treasury bills, reserve bank rates, chartered banks rates, government bonds in the short or the medium or the long term field-and in every case you can find a differential, and over the long years there has always existed this difference as between rates in Canada and in the United States. There is nothing new in the present situation, and hon. members
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).1
who try to make it appear that there is something new in this situation are, whether wittingly or unwittingly, misleading the public. This is a situation which has existed as long as Canada has existed, and it should not be misrepresented.
Then the statement was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that in permitting the banks which have taken this one-year treasury bill to include it in their 7 per cent reserve we are indulging in something highly inflationary. It is regrettable that the hon. member does not appreciate what inflation is. This is the same hon. member who was chastising the government a few days ago with regard to the tightness of money. Now he is saying, if his statement has any meaning at all, that we should not permit the banks to include their holdings of this one-year treasury bill in their 7 per cent reserve.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member did not mean that, his statement was without relevance or significance to the matter that he was discussing.
To the extent to which chartered banks turn in holdings of this government bond maturing on July 1 and replace it with the 12-month treasury bill they will, as I pointed out in reply to the question of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River last night, be permitted to include this new obligation in their 7 per cent reserve holding, which they could not do before in the case of the bonds; but that is not an inflationary tactic at all. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman is contending that the rules in respect of what may be counted in the 7 per cent reserve should be tightened, then he in fact is proposing a tighter money policy.
Then he goes on to talk about the government putting its faith in the market place. Mr. Chairman, the government has to deal with the public to the extent to which the public holds its government obligations. We have to deal with those who are the creditors of the treasury, the people who have acquired those obligations. It is so interesting to hear this necessary process described as putting faith in the market place and being worthy only of the hon. member's denunciation. He says we should do something else. What is the something else? The only other thing, Mr. Chairman, is to turn loose the printing presses and debauch the currency, or to take the money from the people by compulsory means and that means harsh taxation or confiscation. This government does not propose to pursue any of those courses.
What about taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Therefore, I invite the hon. member to ponder well on this fact, that the government of that province which to him and those in his party who think like him is regarded as their paradise, the province of Saskatchewan, has done its financing in the market place and believe me, not so much in the market place of Canada as in the market place in New York. In the thinking of the hon. member it is all very well for the government of Saskatchewan to do these things and even to do them in New York. I am not criticizing the policy of the Saskatchewan government in this regard at all, but I do invite the hon. member to ponder well on why he castigates the federal government for dealing in precisely the same way with those who are its creditors in this country.
He is raising more bogeys today. He raised the bogey of an amendment to the Bank Act to raise the rate, an amendment to the National Housing Act to raise the rate. He has been told in this house, within the last week no less, that the government does not propose to introduce any amendments at this session to either of those acts, but he goes on raising those senseless bogeys.
Probably the last of those curious fallacies, those unique fallacies of the hon. member was his reference to the exchange rate as between the Canadian dollar and the United States dollar, and its bearing upon wider considerations affecting trade and the economies of the two countries. Mr. Chairman, I am not going to review the factors that enter into the present exchange rate. I did that in a recent debate in this house. Today the Canadian dollar is at a premium of approximately four cents over the United States dollar; but, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member evidently has quite misapprehended how this exchange differential has arisen as he has misapprehended the effect that it has on the terms of trade between Canada and the United States.
I doubt whether we shall hear a more extraordinary statement than the one he made this afternoon, namely that because of the existence of this premium Canadians had, as I understood him to say, last year paid a billion dollars more to the United States than they would otherwise have done.
No, I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very hard to follow the hon. member in what he has to say.

I am convinced the minister would not want to misrepresent me. I said the profits, the dividends and the interest rates that were paid by the Canadian economy last

year on United States investments in Canada exceeded a billion dollars. It had nothing to do with the value of the Canadian dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it would be very interesting indeed to see the hon. member produce the evidence upon which he bases that statement. You see, Mr. Chairman, it would require the assumption that there was moving across the Canadian border in terms of exchange translated into the exchange of the other country something over, I suppose, $25 billion, to have the difference in the exchange which varied throughout the year but averaged out at something like 3J per cent, I suppose, for the whole 12 months, amount to $1 billion. However, it is a fantastic statement. The gross investment of United States capital in Canada is about $18 billion. The net is substantially less. The net United States investment in Canada today is approximately-I think if I said about $13 billion I would be pretty close to the mark. Evidently, the hon. member just takes all of the United States investment in Canada, adds to it substantially and then calculates the exchange rate on that and assumes that the whole amount moved across the border, and was changed from the currency of one country to the currency of the other country in one year. How utterly and sadly fantastic and, Mr. Chairman, we have to sit here and listen to such things in the Canadian House of Commons!
I did not say anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very hard to understand what the hon. member does mean.
I will agree with that; it is hard for the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very pleased to receive that generous absolution at the hands of the hon. member. One final observation, Mr. Chairman-
Not final!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Final for the time being. The hon. member for Welland, back on his favourite theme preaching gloom and making things look as black as possible, and hurting the country's credit just as much as gloomy and erroneous statements can hurt it-
Why say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -said that interest rates were going up week after week. I invite the hon. member to ponder on the fact that the rates on our treasury bills were down last week.

That is the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member says yes. Perhaps it would have been a little lair on his part if he had said that when he was speaking earlier-
He did say it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -instead of saying interest rates were going up week after week.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no fairer member than the hon. member for Welland.
On a question of privilege; I did say that last week our interest rates on our 91 treasury bills were down in the market, and the differential with those of the United States was not as large.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member did say also-and 1 took down his words as he said them-that interest rates are going up week after week. There have been periods when they were going up, but why make things worse than they are, why distort the facts, always on the side of gloom? Let us rather, in deference to our duty as Canadians and the responsibility that is shared by all hon. members of this house in relation to the credit of this country, seek not to put an unwarranted gloomy interpretation or colour upon the facts, but let us deal with facts and not with gloom.
When did you develop that high and lofty attitude?
Would the minister permit a question? Did they not go up yesterday when these treasury bills were sold to nearly 5J per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, this is the first offering in this one-year field in the history of Canada.

I regret very much that I have to differ so violently with the minister. I also regret that the minister had to reply almost immediately and that his officials were unable to prepare a speech which he might have been able to deliver because I am convinced that a prepared speech of that kind would have made for much more reasonableness than the one to which we have had to listen. In the first place, the minister again referred to his statement last night when he said, as found on page 4278 of Hansard, that the $200 million "has been very heavily oversubscribed". The minister knows very well that when you offer treasury bills there is just no such animal as oversubscription.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense.

There are offers of many kinds and varied amounts, and the government accepts $200 million of the best offers that are being made. It is simply ridiculous to claim

that there was an oversubscription of an offering of treasury bills because, having regard to the way in which treasury bills are marketed, it is absolutely impossible for anyone ever to claim that an offering was heavily oversubscribed or even in any way oversubscribed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is nonsense.

I give the minister full marks for having the best interests of the Canadian people at heart, and I assume that when these offerings were opened yesterday at 5 p.m., I believe, the minister's advisers placed before him the $200 million of offerings with the lowest effective yield and the minister accepted them. There may well have been $1 billion or $5 billion offered to the minister. However, if he had accepted any of these other offers he would have had to pay a higher rate. I do not think the minister is able to argue successfully that the offering of treasury bills was heavily oversubscribed. We have never heard this terminology before with regard to treasury bills. When bonds are offered bearing a fixed rate of interest we can easily have oversubscription. When the government offers at par Canada savings bonds bearing a fixed rate of interest and having a fixed price there may be oversubscription. However, there never is oversubscription when you offer anything on the auction block.
I am not going to use terms that the minister loves to use such as "unadulterated nonsense". I thought he had forgotten that the other day when he only said that I was mixed up. I thought the minister was making considerable progress in his use of language with regard to opinions expressed by the opposition. However, the minister made one very serious error when he implied, I think even more than implied, that we in this group take satisfaction in a lack of faith in the government on the part of the Canadian people. I must inform the minister immediately that the only reason I am here and the only reason I rise at this time is not to express any satisfaction but to express our regrets at the lack of faith. I am attempting in my own humble way to advocate remedies which will restore the faith of the Canadian people in the monetary policy that the government of the day is pursuing.
I know that if you say a thing often enough maybe enough of the voters will believe you and the minister again expressed his belief that there was a heavy demand on the money available today. Again I must ask him, who is exercising the heavy demand? Is it the industrial heart of Canada? Is it the consumers of Canada or is it the minister himself who is exerting the heavy demand? I

should like to refer to the announcement made a little while ago by the banks of Canada. As if by magic, according to the interpretation of the minister, the banks of Canada announced at the same time that it was necessary to curtail the issuance of credit for the expansion of Canadian enterprise. I would point out that it was none other than the Minister of Finance who expressed his needs to the banking institutions of Canada in no uncertain terms and who impressed upon the banks that his needs ought to come first as they were of so much greater importance and that the expansion of the Canadian economy ought to take a secondary role.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was never said.

The minister, of course, completely ignored the main tenor of my remarks in which I asked the minister where he expected to obtain the rest of the capital needs of the government. Some $1,800 million has to be raised before March 31 next. He has already had to pay an interest rate of 4.49 per cent on his initial issue, so what kind of interest rate may he well have to offer before March 31 next?
The minister also went to great length to explain the difference between rates on issues for which he is responsible and on the offerings of the United States government. He indicated yesterday that an offering almost like the one that he put out yesterday, a one-year United States treasury bill, produced a yield of 4.05 per cent. I assume that is in terms of United States dollars which means that in terms of Canadian dollars the yield would be slightly under 4 per cent. However, the money invested is United States money so it would be 4.05 per cent. For years now our dollar has been worth more than the United States dollar and we fail to understand why an offering by the Canadian Minister of Finance should have to pay an effective rate of 4.49 per cent when south of the border, where their money is worth less, they are able to obtain money for 4.05 per cent.
The minister was very mixed up in his interpretation of the billion dollars that has to leave Canada to pay homage to United States investment in Canada. It had nothing whatever to do with the fact that our dollar is worth more than the United States dollar. I simply reminded the minister of the information that has been available on the financial pages of the newspapers for several months that out of the 1958 Canadian economy there had to be paid to United States investors in Canada, by way of earnings on United
Interim Supply
States investment in Canada, by way of interest rates on United States holdings of Canadian securities, a sum of money in excess of a billion dollars. The minister, himself, by listing United States investments in Canada tended to confirm these newspaper reports. He indicated that there was invested in Canada by United States investors a sum of money in excess of $18,000 million, and the return on that is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 4.5 per cent. I am not saying the return is excessive at all.
However, I am attempting to point out that the failure of the government of Canada to supply leadership to the Canadian people, to supply the incentive to the Canadian people to be responsible for the development of Canadian enterprise, the failure of their leadership to appeal to the patriotism of the Canadian people to have confidence in the Canada of tomorrow, leads us to rely more and more for our prosperity on the confidence and faith that others have in us and in our resources. This places us ever more in hock to outside interests. The longer this condition is permitted to continue, the longer we are postponing the event. Some day Shylock will demand his pound of flesh and the Canadian people will suffer the consequence. I know that this is not peculiar to the federal Minister of Finance. Almost all levels of government and very certainly most individual Canadians are living beyond their means. However, hitherto the federal ministers of finance have been the prime leaders in sponsoring the philosophy that we can continue to borrow to keep pace with eternal prosperity. Those days must end, and they will end.
The sooner that Canadians in all walks of life, under the leadership of the Minister of Finance, begin to realize that we have to buy for the growing boy a new set of breeches every year, that if necessary we have to reduce our expenditures in order that we might eventually own Canada ourselves, the better off we will be. However, the minister continues to place blind reliance on the money market, puts his head in the sand and hopes that maybe tomorrow the sun will shine. He compares himself with the minister of finance of Saskatchewan. There simply is no comparison between the authority and power of this federal Minister of Finance and the authority and power of the minister of finance of any province. I believe even the minister will agree that compared to other provinces, the minister of finance of Saskatchewan, Mr. Fines, has done well indeed.
The minister asks, what is our remedy? He offers what he imagines is our remedy. He says, by implication at least, that the
C.C.F. is advocating we use the printing press.
I believe the Minister of Finance knows

Interim Supply
better than that. Throughout its entire history, while the C.C.F. has advocated monetary reform, it has never advocated turning the handle of the printing press and turning out money for which there is no value. There is only one political movement of which I know that has advocated that, and that is the Social Credit movement. Let me warn the minister that if he pursues his present course of action, those irresponsible advocates of monetary reform are going to grow in influence throughout Canada. I am very annoyed, and I regret very much the evidence of the growth of a movement such as the Union des Electeurs in Quebec, where they are able to persuade municipality after municipality that the minister should use the Bank of Canada to finance, without interest, all the capital needs of our municipal governments. The list of municipalities advocating this measure is becoming alarmingly large.
This is an irresponsible recommendation and the minister well knows it is irresponsible. However, if the minister is going to follow his reactionary policies these counter movements are going to grow. You will find one city council after another throughout Canada endorsing the submissions of the Union des Electeurs. We have never advocated the issuance of more currency than is necessary to meet the needs of the Canadian economy. However, we have asked the minister to make a survey by means of a national investment board, royal commission or otherwise-let him decide whatever means he thinks best- of the credit resources available within the Canadian economy. We have asked for a survey of the credit needs of the various levels of government in Canada, of industrial enterprises and of individuals in Canada. The minister has, hitherto, laughed off all these recommendations.
I should like to spend many minutes more in offering many other recommendations as to how the minister might undertake measures that would relieve him of the very difficult situation in which I think he ought to admit he is. Our submission is that the sooner the minister admits he is in difficulty, the sooner we will begin to find a solution and, as real Canadians we will work our way out of the predicament in which we are now.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house now for third reading is a much different and much improved bill from that presented to the house by the government. It will be recalled that at the second reading of the bill,

when the principle was before the house for approval, the opposition agreed to the principle of the bill, namely that a national energy board be set up to deal with oil and gas pipe lines, the export of gas and power and certain related matters. But at that stage they opposed certain clauses in the bill; as a matter of fact they opposed strongly some of the individual clauses. The opposition argued that they were contrary to the type of provisions that should be in such a bill and indeed wrong in principle in many cases.
The main items we opposed on the second reading when we were approving the principle of the bill may be summarized in this way. I will not attempt to deal with them all but only with the main ones. We opposed the duplication of government services which we thought was inherent in the wide advisory powers given to the energy board under clause 22 of the bill. In other words, we argued that the board would be duplicating services already performed by such government agencies as the atomic energy control board, the dominion coal board and other bodies of a similar type.
Then we opposed at some length what we thought were the arbitrary and excessive powers which the minister or the governor in council, as the case may be, was seeking under the bill which was submitted. We thought those powers were quite excessive and that no case could be made out for them. The type of arbitrary power to which I am referring was, for instance, the minister's right to refuse to table reports and studies made by the board on matters of energy under clause 22 (1), that is to say reports and studies that were not of a confidential nature.
Then we opposed the arbitrary power, as we saw it, inherent in clause 49 which was a clause in part III of the bill which deals with the issuance of certificates of public convenience and necessity governing the construction and operation of pipe lines. The arbitrary power we opposed there was the right of the governor in council to exempt lines from certain of the effective clauses in the operation of part III of the bill. A similar power was contained in clause 85 (2) of the bill which permitted the governor in council by regulation to exempt any person or class of persons of any product or class of products or any transactions, persons or areas from the operation of all or any of the provisions of part VI of the bill which was the part having to do with the export and import of gas and power. We argued that that was an arbitrary power that was wrongly being sought by the governor in council.
Then another very important objection to the bill was on clause 87, which had to do
National Energy Board
with the import of oil. There were really two parts to our objection to that clause. There was the same argument as we applied to other arbitrary powers; the governor in council seeking arbitrary powers to impose import controls and quotas on the import of oil. We thought there was no emergency warranting that step and that no case had been made out for it, and we also opposed such an important matter of change in government policy as controlling the import of oil and putting an embargo upon it being decided by the governor in council. We argued that it should be determined by parliament before any such far-reaching step was taken.
On second reading we also requested that the bill go to a standing committee. I still adhere to that view, but it is neither here nor there now because we were voted down on it and our request was not acceded to. We thought and still think it was the type of bill which should have gone to a standing committee. There were many clauses in the bill which could have been better drafted by a standing committee, but as I say our request was not acceded to.
At the committee stage of the bill a great many amendments were put forward. I think there were some 30 in all. Seventeen amendments were adopted, 11 were rejected and two were withdrawn. But the effect of those amendments was very important. We think that those amendments materially improved the bill. Some of them went very far in removing our objections to specific clauses of the bill. Perhaps in fairness I should deal with some of these amendments, not in a detailed way, but in order to make my point. We did put forward an important amendment to reduce the number of members of the board from five to three. We thought that would make for a better board, a stronger board in all the circumstances bearing in mind the volume and nature of the work and the difficulty in securing an adequate number of able men. But the committee in its wisdom unfortunately rejected that request.
Then we put forward another amendment which we thought was of considerable importance but which was also rejected. That amendment had to do with a provision in clause 83 of the bill. It will be recalled that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on second reading spoke about the desirability of being sure that in the export of gas the price charged by exporters to the United States was not less than that charged to
430G

National Energy Board Canadians in like conditions. The Prime Minister's remarks will be found at the bottom of page 4025 of Hansard for May 26 last, where he said:
As to the price to be charged for gas and power, it must be just and reasonable in relation to the public interests. With the implementation of this legislation, no longer will there be any suspicion that the Canadian consumer is being forced to subsidize the foreign markets or that Canadian industries will be asked to pay higher prices for their industries-
I think there is a printer's error there and it should read "energy".
-than those paid by foreign industries using Canadian energy.
We thought the bill should have such a safeguard in it and we put forward an amendment to clause 83 (b) to that effect. Clause 83 (b) is the clause having to do with an application to the board for a licence to export, and it was argued in committee that that matter was adequately taken care of by the provision in the clause as it stood, namely:
-board shall satisfy itself that
(b) the price to be charged by an applicant for gas or power exported by him is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
The government argued that that provision adequately took care of the situation and our amendment was rejected. We did not quite agree with that view, but in any event the amendment was rejected. But we do think now that in the light of the discussion on that point at the committee stage it is highly probable that the board, in interpreting the meaning of the words "just and reasonable", is likely to take some notice of the argument advanced on this clause in the committee stage and is likely to try to apply that criterion as far as it can. For that reason I am making no more of our suggested amendment at this point. I think it was a correct amendment and I regret it was not accepted; but we think, having regard to all the circumstances, that the board will probably take cognizance of it anyway under the requirement that they shall satisfy themselves that the price to be charged is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest. The bill still does not do in so many words what the Prime Minister claimed it would do in this respect; but that is a point which does not fall to be argued here.
As to amendments which were adopted, may I say this. First of all there was our objection to the arbitrary powers which I mentioned a moment ago contained in clause 49 of the bill. That is the clause permitting the governor in council to exempt lines from the operation of part III of the bill; that is the part having to do with certificates of
[Mr. Mcllraith.j
public convenience and necessity in the construction and operation of pipe lines. That arbitrary power was removed from the bill in the committee stage. The government acceded to that, and I am not sure that they did not take our criticism and put it in the form of an amendment themselves. In any event, they acceded to our request and it was embodied in an amendment and that objectionable feature was removed from that clause.
Then there was the arbitrary power contained in clause 85 (2), which had the effect, we thought, of permitting the governor in council by regulation virtually to exempt gas pipe lines and gas exporters from the operation of the export provisions of the bill. We felt very strongly about that and so argued, and the government accepted an amendment which removed that objectionable subclause completely from the bill. It is quite true that a much more limited subclause was put in clause 87 relating to oil.
When we are dealing with oil products, there are, of course, a great variety of products and it is difficult to envisage any circumstance in which anyone would want to bring all of them under control; and while there might still be a case made for arguing against the arbitrary power of that clause, it is a very much more limited power and a case can be made for its retention, and I make no more of that point. The main point we were making was achieved by the removal of subclause (2) of clause 85.
Then, when we come to clause 87, the clause permitting the governor in council by declaration to extend the application of the bill to oil-to provide for regulation and control of oil imports and exports-we advanced a somewhat extensive argument. I sought to develop it as some length; I will not repeat what was said on that occasion, because it can be found on page 4028 of Hansard. But we did put forward arguments on two grounds. One of those grounds was the improper granting of arbitrary power. The other was that a decision of this nature was so important and so far-reaching in relation to trade policy that no action should be taken other than by a decision of parliament, and that parliament should have control of this matter. We maintained that there was no foreseeable situation in which there would not be sufficient time for parliament to deal with the subject should the need ever arise. We addressed ourselves, also, to a remark which the minister made as reported at page 3929 of Hansard when presenting the bill for second reading, on which occasion he said:
The case with respect to licensing imports of oil is different and more complicated. I do not propose to argue the case fully today. It would be

premature to do so until the second report of the Borden commission in respect of this matter has been received and considered.
We objected to the clause in the light of that statement, too. In any event, our arguments and objections on that point were recognized by the government, and the government, of its own volition, after our views had been expressed, brought forward an amendment which, while it did not fully meet the situation as we saw it, did go a very long way toward meeting our objection. Although the clause as amended does not permit parliament to make the original decision as to whether or not import control should be applied to oil, it does provide that if the government makes such a decision parliament shall have the opportunity of debating the matter promptly and of revoking the decision taken. So that while this could,
I suppose, properly be called second best from the point of view of our argument, it does go a very long way toward meeting our wishes on that point, and materially improves the bill.
I have sought to deal with this subject fairly briefly at this stage, and I have endeavoured not to reopen old arguments. I think I have been fair in picking out only those amendments which best serve to illustrate the point I am seeking to make. There were a great many other amendments which I could deal with, some of them of considerable importance, but though they are important they do not illustrate the point I have in mind.
I may say that had the amendments with which I have been dealing not been accepted in committee I do not see how we could now accept the whole bill as it would have been presented to us. However, these amendments having been made, and having gone so far toward meeting the objections we raised, we believe that on balance the bill is very markedly improved. The adoption of 17 amendments goes a very long way in improving the measure. I do not suppose I ought to comment on the work which was done in committee-work in which I, myself, participated-but I think all hon. members will agree that the bill has been improved as compared with the form in which it was first introduced.
We on this side have been sharply critical of the government for not enunciating its policy on this important subject earlier. Now that this policy has finally been announced and the present measure presented to parliament; now that the discussion in committee has been completed, and the situation in the country and in the industry being such that action should be promptly taken, we feel that no useful or proper purpose would be
National Energy Board
served by our presenting any amendments on third reading. While we have some reservations about certain parts of the bill, we think it is sufficiently improved for us to be able to concur in the third reading at this time and we hope that the government, when the bill has passed through all its stages, will proclaim it immediately and set about the task, which I think will probably be a difficult one, of finding as competent a board as it can to exercise the powers granted by this legislation.
In this, we hope the government will be successful, because the influence of the board on the industry itself and on the economy of the country as a whole will be substantial. We, therefore, in the light of the explanations I have made, are prepared to accord third reading to the bill.
