speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the basic position of the three parties in the house has not materially changed since second reading. The Liberal party voted for second reading of the bill. They are now more in agreement with that vote than they were when they made it, so that on third reading they are very much in favour of this legislation.
As far as we are concerned, we acknowledge that certain improvements have been made. We are pleased that the government has gone some distance toward improving the legislation which was brought before this house, and we are aware that the government has acknowledged, in moving certain amendments, the role played by opposition members in advancing various propositions and in making certain criticisms of the measure as originally brought down.
However, our fundamental objection remains; namely that under this legislation the consumers of this country, both householders and industry, will pay higher prices for natural gas and for oil than are necessary. The role of the federal government in this field should have been a more positive one, a more active one, and one which would have resulted in the lowering of costs of energy to Canadians consumers and Canadian industry.
We are still very much concerned that the government has failed to implement the recommendation of the Borden commission that, in proceeding with the setting up of an energy board and the establishment of rates, a return on the shareholders' equity alone should be considered, and not a net return on all the assets of a corporation which would result in a much greater return on the shareholders' equity. The failure
4302	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board
of the government to implement that proposition in the legislation as guidance to the board, will, of course, mean higher prices for gas and oil in the future.
There are certain clauses in the bill which have been improved, and these have been outlined very thoroughly by the hon. member for Ottawa West. In our opinion, while the government has agreed to a certain curtailment of the all-embracing power for which provision was originally made in this bill, there are still too many examples of instances where the government has retained arbitrary powers for itself. I might refer, in particular, to clause 44 which reads:
The board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line-
I could refer to clause 47:
Subject to subsection 2, the board may by order, with the approval of the governor in council, revoke or suspend a certificate if, in the opinion of the board, the person to whom it was issued has violated or failed to comply with any term or condition thereof.
We feel that in a case of wrongdoing or failure to abide by the terms of a certificate, power should not be retained by the governor in council to allow the company to break the terms of its certificate and still remain in existence without a penalty being provided. This could lead to very great abuses; it could lead to favouritism and it could lead to a type of pork barrel by a government that wished to play favourites under certain conditions.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we acknowledge certain substantial improvements in the bill, but there are certain provisions still remaining that we feel should have been improved by the committee. Clause 61 of the bill is not the only one that gives us concern, but is it one that is very ill-defined and has not been adequately explained by the minister. It reads as follows:
Where the gas transmitted by a company through its pipe line from any place within a province to any place outside the province is the property of the company, such proportion as the board may fix of the differential between the amount paid by the company for the gas and the amount for which the gas is sold by the company shall for the purposes of this part be deemed to be a toll charged by the company to the purchaser for the transmission thereof.
In other words, under clause 61, it is not necessary for the board to control the difference between the cost of gas going into a pipe line and the price of gas coming out of a pipe line but only an undefined portion of that difference, which might, in the opinion of the board, be a very small part of the difference, and therefore it might 

result in very ineffective and inadequate action by the board in controlling tolls for the transmission of gas.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we think the government should have presented an alternative policy to this house. Not only should the board have had more exact instructions, not only should the governor in council have had less power to set aside decisions of the board, not only should profits and returns have been confined to shareholders' equity, but once again we say that in our opinion a public utility such as this, something that is a natural monopoly, is a field for public ownership, no matter what the political theories of any political party may be, a form of ownership which would give to the Canadian consumer energy at the lowest possible price.

speechtext:
Having expressed, in the first part of his speech opinions which, coming from him, have a hollow sound because they are so new, and which, I readily recognize, are in accordance with the doctrine of fiscal autonomy we have been preaching for years,
Dominion-Provincial Relations the hon. member for Laurier attempted to show inconsistencies in our position and, in a thunderous voice, as I am told, he urged us to vote against a measure which, I must point out, originated back in the days when the Liberal party was in office.
What a strange logic. There is the result of the efforts he has been making-quite in vain-since his return to politics, to speak on behalf of the province of Quebec. Obviously, it is no easy task for him to shed his past, after he has had a share in the works of the federal government, with astonishing regularity and continuity, throughout the dark days when the provinces stood at the mercy of the decisions and dictates of its leaders, who rebuffed with scornful mockery anyone who dared to seek fiscal freedom for the provinces and thus sought to insure the upholding and respect of the constitution without which Canada, as it now exists, would have been no more than a marvelous Utopia.
The latter part of the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier, where he implies that Quebec Conservatives are renegades and threatens them with electoral come-uppance, conjured up in my memory a short story by Villiers de l'lsle Adam entitled Plagiaries of Thunder. The action took place in a faraway island where some huge aras, an Australian species of macaws, felt they could spread terror by imitating the thunder. One day an eagle happened by, recognized them and terrified them. The aras attempted rather unsuccessfully, to imitate the cry of the eagle, but could not from then on frighten the inhabitants of the island who had by now realized that, after all, the would-be eagles were mere parrots.
By this comparison I do not wish to minimize the merits and the high qualities of the hon. member for Laurier. But I want to tell him that his pronouncements on autonomy are, as far as I am concerned, strongly reminiscent of this story, and that we Quebec Conservatives will surely not allow ourselves to be frightened by plagiaries of thunder, whoever they may be and whencesoever they may come from.
The bill introduced today by the government is after all but the fulfilment of the following promise made in the speech from the throne:
My government will recommend an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for another year the increase made last year in the provincial share of personal income tax revenue.
In other words, the purpose of this bill is to maintain the 13 per cent income tax de-
4304	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations ductions granted to the taxpayers of the provinces where a similar tax is already levied.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in saying, without any feeling of repudiating my convictions, that I am happy to support this bill for several reasons, particularly because it clearly renews the recognition of the constitutional right of the provinces to tax incomes and to exercise this right freely. The hon. members of the house know the origin of this bill. Last year, I had the opportunity to recall the battles that certain provinces have had to wage against the federal government since the war to obtain practical recognition of the exercise of a right which is specifically and clearly expressed in the Constitutional Act of 1867.
I have referred to the high-handed and uncompromising way in which some of them were treated at the federal-provincial conferences held between 1940 and 1956. I do not intend to go over this particularly tragical phase of the relations between the federal government and the provinces, during which our friends of the opposition were far from having those feelings of autonomy that they so glibly talk about now that they no longer have the responsibility of power. To keep within the limits of this legislation, I would like to relate briefly how the government of the day was compelled to change its mind and to adopt the act 4-5 Elizabeth 11(1956) the beneficial results of which are only increased and extended under this bill.
During the provincial session of 1953-1954, the Quebec government which, until then and as was strictly within its rights, had refused to renew the tax arrangements passed with the federal government during the war, decided to set up a provincial income tax, thus affirming a constitutional and undeniable right. As a result and because the province was exercising a right which is essential to its freedom in matters of taxation, a number of taxpayers had to pay double tribute to the fiscal authorities.
What was then the position of the government, the surviving members of which now set themselves up as champions of provincial autonomy? What theory was to guide those who, during each election, kept on recalling in the province of Quebec the illustrious memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier? Were they going at last to be guided by the ideas of that great leader who, as early as 1905, had said here in the House of Commons:


It is a sound principle of finance, and a still sounder principle of government, that those who have the duty of expending the revenue of a country should also be saddled with the responsibility of levying and providing it.
Alas no! It must be said that the prime minister of this country was far from having in the province of Quebec assistants of his own calibre. Mr. Lesage, for one, far from recognizing the rights of the provinces, did not care a fig for them when, in April, 1954, he said:
This double taxation is exclusively due to the decision of the Quebec government which now attempts to throw the blame upon the Canadian government. This reminds me of the little boy-
Mind you, I am still quoting-
[DOT]-who pulled the cat's tail and replied to his father, who had told him to stop: "I am not doing the pulling: the cat is."
Not content with that quip of questionable taste, he went so far as to set himself up as a prophet and went on to say:
Some would lay down as a principle that any province which has not signed an agreement should be entitled to levy deductible taxes in proportion to the amount it would receive under the agreements . . . We can already see-[DOT]
Continued Mr. Lesage-
-the tremendous confusion that would follow the application of that principle subscribed to by the Conservatives at their last convention.
Of course, at that time Mr. Lesage never thought that the first one who would apply, at least in part, that Conservative policy would be none other than his own leader, Mr. Louis St. Laurent who, two years later, reducing to silence the small politicians surrounding him, putting aside all narrow, mean and political considerations, became the instigator of the 4-5 Elizabeth II act, chapter 29, adopted on January 31, 1956. Well, Mr. Speaker, that act is at the very origin of the bill that is introduced today, in which the principle of deduction is quite clearly stated.
I have read with interest the debate that has been held on that legislation. I have looked in vain for what was said on that occasion by the hon. member for Laurier and the other Liberal members of the province of Quebec. They were completely mum. Not one of those who, today, in the opposition, want to show us the way and who try to criticize our attitudes, not one of them has risen to denounce the remarks made two years earlier by Mr. Lesage, or at least to tone them down. Not one of them dared state the autonomist argument so loudly upheld by the hon. member for Laurier now that he is in the opposition.

In order to defend the conciliating attitude of Mr. St. Laurent and justify his new policy -a Conservative policy, according to Mr. Lesage-they had to resort to Mr. Walter Tucker, former Liberal chief of Saskatchewan and then Liberal member for Rosthern, whose speech was to be a source of inspiration for our friends opposite.
On that same occasion, the members of the Conservative opposition did not fail to make statements which are and I trust always will be a source of inspiration for this government. Thus, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), recalled in clear and precise language that left no room for doubt the theory denounced two years before by Mr. Lesage and his friends, and which their leader, Mr. St. Laurent, was at that time consecrating by legislation with regard to individual and corporation income taxes.
(Text):
When this field Is entered into or when negotiations are entered upon with a view to arriving at understandings or divisions of the fields of taxation between the dominion and provincial authorities, let us remember, as the dominion government is prone to forget, that the provinces are in those fields not by leave of anyone; they are there as of right. It is their constitutional right. When there are suggestions from the dominion government about allowing the provinces to occupy some of this field, referring to that as a concession, we have a measure, Mr. Speaker, of the error in the federal government's thinking.
(Translation):
The present Speaker of the house will allow me to recall what he himself said on that occasion:
(Text):
I think those who believe that the federal system means something in this country and should be preserved owe a great deal to the fortitude of the people of Quebec, who have maintained that position throughout the last 10 years since the war. But even Quebec felt the pinch of the conditions with which they were confronted, and in 1954 and 1955 met something of a crisis which required the province to levy income taxes of their own, something which proved to be an embarrassment to them, and certainly to the federal government, and which resulted in a concession from Ottawa, namely a 10 per cent abatement in the personal income tax field. I think that is probably the genesis of the new agreements or the new arrangements which are now under consideration.
(Translation):
That new trend in the fiscal policy of the federal government was to become still more pronounced and definite with the coming to power of the Conservative administration. In that same debate, the man who is now the head of this nation had forecast it as follows:
Dominion-Provincial Relations
(Text):
When I go back to 1945 I remember the great hopes that were held; and I am in agreement with my hon. friend the minister in this regard that the matter is complex. It is one of the most difficult problems that parliament, or the government, can be called upon to deal with, because there are so many facets, so many difficulties and so many situations that demand not an arbitrary attitude but a compromising and considered one.
(Translation):
And later, admitting that that legislation was a step in the right direction, he added:
(Text):
Under our constitution the provinces were never intended to be beggars. The provinces have responsibilities, the provinces have fields of action, and the concentration of power and authority in the federal government with respect to taxation has had an adverse effect.
(Translation):
Such was the spirit which, under the new regime, was to form the basis of the relations between the federal state and the provincial governments. That spirit, all provincial governments at the 1957 conference were able to note and to appreciate, and give credit for it to this government. They realized that the atmosphere had changed, that they were entering upon a new era, that the provinces, from then on, would no longer be considered as vassals, obliged to bow to the federal state's will and demands.
After two days of discussion, before they separated, the representatives of the country and of the provinces who had taken part in those meetings agreed on the text of a press communique which included the following paragraph;
Possible changes in the Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act were discussed, but it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach conclusion on this matter prior to further consideration of the subject by the dominion government, in the light of the public statement made by the provincial representatives in open sessions and the discussions which took place in committee.
In other words, since from then on conclusions would no more precede but follow discussions, since from then on, to reach those conclusions, the ten provinces as well as the federal state would be entitled to express their opinion, we could no longer afford the luxury of improvisation and hasty action. Besides, the law of January 1956 covered a five-year period, which has not yet expired. Meanwhile, as early as January 1958, this government hastened to increase that portion of taxes to be paid to the provinces, and to increase from 10 to 13 per cent the income tax deduction for the taxpayers of provinces that exercise their own power of taxation.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Considering the importance of the problem and the impact that a slap-dash solution might bring about, the government tried to avoid hasty steps. At the second but last conference, at the suggestion of Mr. Frost and by common agreement, a committee was formed made up of federal and provincial officials to study technical problems raised by fiscal and economic relations between the various governments. On January 15 last, the Prime Minister announced that recourse would be had to this committee to prepare a conference of finance ministers of the various provinces under the chairmanship of the federal Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to say, in the budget debate, how this policy seemed wise and forward-looking, in my opinion. The conference will make it possible to probe several aspects of this far-reaching problem of taxation in Canada. It will give rise to exchanges of views which are essential and which, I am sure, are such as to create an atmosphere of good will and understanding which is a necessity in a country with a constitutional organization such as ours.
In view of the abundance and variety of legislation, both at the federal and provincial level, in view of the frictions that are likely to occur from time to time, this conference will, I firmly believe, be the first step towards an agreement which, this time, will give due consideration to the requirements of the constitution, to its evolution since 1867, and to the legitimate needs and various views of the provinces and of the federal government.
This, Mr. Speaker, explains why and in what spirit I shall heartily vote in favour of the bill placed before us today by the Minister of Finance, convinced as I am that in so doing, far from transgressing any principles and convictions, I shall be doing my bit-in a very modest way, I realize- for the welfare and progress of the Canadian nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to understand why the government's answer to the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) should be entrusted to someone who is not a member of the cabinet. I would have thought that a minister from the province of Quebec would have answered the statements of my colleague, the hon. member for Laurier, especially following his statements last night when he said, as found on page 4277 of Hansard:
As may be noted, Mr. Speaker, the election promises made by the Conservative party in the field of fiscal relations in 1957 and 1958 have been completely disallowed. The Conservative government, far from treating the provinces with more generosity than did the Liberals, as it had promised, takes over a greater share of direct taxation. It completely ignores the concrete proposals put forward by the majority of provincial premiers in November 1957. More than that, it even refuses to meet them again.
And finally my colleague said:
It is for all those reasons that the Conservative members from Quebec should now have the courage of their convictions and denounce such betrayal. They must do so, in the name of their principles: they must do so on account of the solemn pledge they made during the last federal election: they must do so for the sake of their electors to whom they gave that pledge, but they must do so also, and perhaps above all, on account of Mr. Duplessis who is responsible for their presence here in the house.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe those statements made by my colleague deserve an answer from someone who is a member of the cabinet in this government.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I do not question the hon. member for Bellechasse's (Mr. Do-rion) right to speak. He spoke well and I think very highly of him. I respect him very much, but I think that it should be a responsibility of a minister of the Canadian government to reply at once to a speech as momentous as the one we heard last night, especially in view of the speech made last night in North Bay by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I now address myself to the Prime Minister and to the speech he made last night in North Bay.
(Text):
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I thought that the speech of my friend the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) should have been replied to at once by a minister from the province of Quebec. I did not deny that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken was qualified in his own right to express his own views; but it seemed to me that, after the challenge made last night by the hon. member for Laurier, the reply ought to have come from one of the Quebec ministers, particularly in the light of the speech made last night in North Bay by my genial friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Last night when the Prime Minister was in North Bay, he gave the impression that

we were going to have a real dominion-provincial conference. There was no reminder there last night in that happy northern Ontario community of the promise made by the Prime Minister in the elections of 1957 when he told the people of Canada and the people of the province of Quebec that when he became Prime Minister, he would call a dominion-provincial conference and resolve once and for all these fiscal differences between the two senior levels of government. That promise now is gradually, the Prime Minister hopes, evaporating in the clouds, never again to be seen and, he hopes, never again to be referred to. Certainly it was not referred to last night at the meeting in North Bay where, according to the Globe and Mail -and I think that would be an authentic bit of reporting-he made the following statement.
Mr. Diefenbaker said a four-point proposal by the Canadian government would be submitted to the conference. It covers:
1.	The existing fiscal arrangements;
2.	Future problems of fiscal arrangements and possible alternative approaches;
3.	Economic and fiscal policies and their impact on intergovernmental financial relations;
4.	Examination of the fiscal and economic outlook.
Then the Prime Minister went on to talk about national problems. I am sure that as a result of that speech many of the mayors concluded that there is going to be not a conference of the new order, of the new character with a new look but the kind of conference that was promised by the Prime Minister in the elections of 1957, one that was going to resolve once and for all this problem of fiscal differences between the two senior levels of government. But of course we all know now that we have had no conference. The conference which was held and which lasted for two days was adjourned. It was to be reconvened but it was not reconvened. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), exercising that ingenuity of his, sent a telegram without giving the provinces an opportunity to discuss the terms or the arrangements. Instead, the government may decide not on a conference of governments but on a study group, a seminar, as the Prime Minister indicated last night. We are going to have a conference- although this he did not explain-of officials. He did not explain that. He said, "We are going to have a conference and we are going to deal with these four subjects". He did not say that what we were going to have was simply a study group, a conference of officials which is nothing more, I submit, than a new delaying tactic devised by this government in the face of its heavy deficit position and more particularly at this
Dominion-Provincial Relations time devised so that it would not embarrass the premier of Ontario who is engaged in a provincial election.

speechtext: Premier Frost has said that he wants another $115 million from this government. He wants it on the basis of a proposal that is now agreed to and supported by all of the provinces, namely on the basis of the new formula, 15-15-50. But because the Minister of Finance and his colleagues would be embarrassed if they were to accede to this request of the premier of Ontario I suppose, politically, they would say at this stage "We cannot accede to your request for $115 million", they have devised the new tactic of having a study group that is going to take place after the provincial election is held in Ontario on June 11 next.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
That is a pet theory of theirs;
I refer to study groups.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: No wonder the Winnipeg Free Press in an editorial dated Wednesday, May 27 had this to say about the situation which has resulted from Mr. Frost's demand for more money which was not acknowledged by the federal government, particularly in the face of the other demands made on the federal government by other provincial governments, and particularly at a time when provincial elections in the province of Ontario are taking place.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It sounds as though the federal Liberals are going to try to help out the Ontario Liberals after all, although not financially.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: The hon. member for Oxford may be very much interested in this matter because he comes from Ontario. I am sure he supports the request of the premier of Ontario for more money from the federal exchequer. I give my hon. friend a chance to say whether or not he supports Premier Frost in his demand for another $115 million. From his silence I take it that he does not acknowledge the offer of an opportunity to indicate this intention but that he joins with me in looking upon this particular demand of Premier Frost indeed as an extremely embarrassing one for this government and also extremely embarrassing at this time for the premier of Ontario.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Then you are supporting Mr. Wintermeyer?

Dominion-Provincial Relations

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Yes. I am supporting the man who I think is likely to be the next premier of the province of Ontario.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Here is what the
Winnipeg Free Press said:
At an election meeting in Peterborough the other night, the premier of Ontario again put on the record what he hopes to get from the Conservative government at Ottawa through the dominion-provincial tax-sharing arrangements. Mr. Frost told the meeting that he was still going after Ottawa for $115 million of tax money. ''I haven't forgotten it", he said. "A country lawyer hangs onto a thing like a pup to a root".
Ontario Conservatives may applaud Mr. Frost's tenacity;-
Says the Winnipeg Free Press.
-but they are unlikely to be joined by Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Fleming. Since the Conservatives came to power in Ottawa, they have carefully avoided a full-dress conference on tax sharing. Their reasons are pretty obvious. Mr. Frost is Mr. Diefenbaker's strongest ally in the provincial field.
I would put in parenthesis-and this is not the Winnipeg Free Press-that perhaps he is not any longer; I do not know. Then the article goes on as follows:
But if the Ontario premier is given what he asks for, what about the other provinces?
Mr. Diefenbaker is firmly committed to the principle of equalization of tax payments. Just a year ago he promised in Parliament that "every province will receive the same treatment" at the dominion-provincial conference.
So an extra $100 million or so tp Mr. Frost would mean proportionately larger payments to the other provinces than they are now getting. But where are the extra hundreds of millions of dollars to come from? The cupboard at Ottawa is bare. Mr. Fleming is now operating with a large annual deficit.
Yet these are the alternatives: Satisfy Mr. Frost and add to the deficit: or leave the Ontario premier still hanging on to his root.
In the circumstances it is little wonder that instead of the full scale conference, Mr. Fleming intends to meet the provincial treasurers in July to talk things over, after which there will be an investigation of federal-provincial relations by experts from Ottawa and the provinces.
This is not, of course, what Mr. Diefenbaker promised-

speechtext: Order. I allowed the hon. member to read a large section of last night's debate before intervening. Now I think he is going to extremes in his reading of the Winnipeg Free Press.

speechtext: While editorial comments are permitted they are to be used with moderation. I trust the hon. member has now read all he wishes.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: There is just one short paragraph which I think would render the whole editorial a little more apparent than otherwise would appear.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: It is a Liberal paper.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
It does not matter where it is from.
This is not, of course, what Mr. Diefenbaker promised before he was elected. But such a conference, or rather the promise of a conference, serves one useful purpose so far as the Conservatives are concerned. It permits Mr. Frost to talk hopefully of an extra $100 millions in tax revenues, without in any way committing Mr. Diefenbaker or Mr. Fleming to do anything about it.
It is not perhaps without some justification that the heading of that editorial is "Mr. Frost's Bone". That is the whole point. This particular device which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) have created is for the very purpose of not embarrassing Mr. Frost, at the same time being able to offer to the mayors and to the public some justification for not having fulfilled an election promise.
I would like to remind the Minister of Finance that this very study that he has in mind can really serve no valuable purpose. Is the study necessary? Certainly when the premiers met at the last conference they dealt with the proposal that there should be a sort of study. I think the words of the former premier of Manitoba in this connection, supported by the premier of Saskatchewan, deserve to be put on the record. What I am now quoting from is the conference proceedings including Mr. Campbell's statement, where he said:
It is the contention of our government that we do not need at this stage to go into a detailed consideration of new principles-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Who is this?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Campbell, a worthy public servant who was entrusted by his people to represent them in the Ontario legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Ontario?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I am sorry, I mean Manitoba. You see, I am so confident about the result in Ontario that I want to elect everybody.
It is the contention of our government that we do not need at this stage to go into a detailed consideration of new principles regarding our fiscal problems. We have gone through all this several times in recent years. We have had a number of meetings on this question. Our officials have met often to discuss its technical aspects.
Then Premier Douglas is reported at page 79 of the proceedings as having said this:
The fundamental failure of the present fiscal arrangements lies not so much in the method of sharing as in the size of the shares themselves.

I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the discussion which took place at that conference between Premier Frost and Mr. Campbell, which will be found at pages 89 to 92 of the proceedings, indicates clearly that they recognize that the present basis of equalization-that is the average per capita yield of the standard tax rates in the two top provinces-had been accepted by the provinces as a workable compromise. There was no question about that as far as all the provinces were concerned. All the provinces are now in favour of the new formula 15-15-50. So the only question which really remains is that of the determination of the standard tax rates, and that is a decision which cannot be made by the officials either of the provinces or of the federal government. That decision can only be made by hon. gentlemen on the ministerial benches who now look at me. That decision cannot be made by the deputy minister of finance or by corresponding officials in the provincial governments. Does the Minister of Finance not agree that that is the only remaining question, as both Mr. Frost and Mr. Campbell indicated?
Therefore to hold such a conference in the face of the fact that these officials cannot make this decision is only to resort to a delaying tactic, so that when my hon. friend presents his next budget he will then be free to indicate something which he now regards as not being free politically to do, namely to say to Mr. Frost, "We cannot accept your further demand of $115 million." That is the only reason for the holding of this conference of officials on July 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: If you knew the facts you would think differently.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I challenge my hon. friend now to indicate I am wrong. I say the only matter now outstanding between the federal government and the provincial governments is to determine the standard rate of tax. That is all that remains, and that cannot be decided by the officials, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance knows that is the case. There is no need any longer for a long study by officials to answer that question. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister never talked about a study. He said, "Elect my party and in the month of September we will call a conference and resolve this question once and for all". That is what he told the people of Canada, and that is what the mayors of Ontario understood him to say last night. By the way, when he met them last night he did
Dominion-Provincial Relations not say anything about calling a conference at which the municipalities would be present.
I see that according to a report in tonight's paper Mr. Mooney, the secretary of that organization, expressed great regret that the Prime Minister would not afford the municipalities the opportunity of participating in a conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Is that the Mr. George Mooney who was a Liberal candidate in a recent federal general election?

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I believe that is the same gentleman, and I may say he is a highly trusted gentleman. My hon. friend endeavours to cast some aspersions not only on that gentleman, but he also seeks to indicate that because a man has been a Liberal candidate he is on that account not to be regarded as a trusted and competent official. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance does not have the same appreciation of Mr. Mooney that others have, he should note that at the conference at which the Prime Minister spoke last night to the mayors of our country thought enough of Mr. Mooney to continue him as secretary of their organization. What the Prime Minister did last night was to say, "Don't worry; we'll look after the municipalities. We realize you have heavy obligations to meet. We will take care of your interests as we sit down at the table with that demanding man, Mr. Frost".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do really enjoy the frivolities, but when the hon. gentleman proceeds to quote what I said in that direction, perhaps he will quote me rather than rely upon his fantastic and imaginative interpretation.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I will very gladly quote what the Prime Minister said, but it will require my looking at the second page of my hon. friend's official journal.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
So that my time shall not be wasted I will ask my colleague to look for it.
The real issue in this situation is that the differences which prevail between the provinces and the federal government have resolved themselves into one single question.
4310	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations That question can only be decided by governments; it cannot and will not be decided by officials. All the facts which will be elicited at a meeting of officials in July will merely confirm, as Premier Douglas and Premier Campbell indicated, what they already have in their treasury offices.
Why does not the Minister of Finance now, before June 11, next Thursday, indicate frankly to the people why there has not been a conference called and why this problem is not finally resolved? Let the Prime Minister be as frank now with the Canadian people and with the parliament of Canada as he was during the election. Let him tell Mr. Frost why he cannot get his $115 million or, if he is going to get it, when he may expect it, instead of continually ignoring parliament and refusing to indicate why a promise solemnly made should not be carried out. Oh, the Prime Minister, that great actor, is obviously very irritated by what I am saying and expresses his irritation by laughter.
When he spoke to the municipalities, this is what he said, this is the report which was made:

We will study this problem, and by the time the study is over the provincial elections in Ontario will be over and we shall be able, afterwards, in a statesmanlike way, to resolve this problem, not in the interests of the Conservative party but in the interests of the people of Canada."

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
That is what the hon. gentleman will say after this conference, and as sure as I am standing here now the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of Finance have no more intention of giving Mr. Frost his additional $100 million than I have of walking across this floor and sitting as a permanent supporter to the right of the Minister of Finance.
Let this government stop dodging this issue. Let them recognize that the only remaining difference is one which governments alone can settle, and let them once and for all face up to this problem of dominion-provincial relations as the government of Canada was expected to do by the electorate when this administration was entrusted with office in June of 1957 and March of 1958.
Mr. Diefenbaker assumed that in the forthcoming conference the provinces would naturally present the viewpoint of the municipalities. There was no indication by the Prime Minister that a federal-provincial-municipal conference would be suitable.
That is not what the Prime Minister told the mayors of Canada; that is not what he said when he told the municipalities: you are poor, and added that the federal government was rich. That is not what he told them during the election. He told them then that he understood their problems and would see to it that assistance was given to them from the federal exchequer to enable them to carry on and discharge their responsibilities. That was not the same thing as the Prime Minister indicated when he stood in Massey Hall in 1957. Mr. Frost put his hand on his shoulder, then and said: "There's my boy; he's going to give me my $115 million
and I am going to see to it that we have a conference where these problems will all be resolved". Mr. Frost was waiting for this conference all last fall, and when, one day, he picked up the Globe and Mail and saw in the speech from the throne that there was not going to be a conference, I presume he called the Prime Minister at once and asked him: "How am I going to get out of this?" Of course, I am imagining some of this. And the Prime Minister said to the Premier of Ontario: "Don't worry, I will get you out of this. Donald is going to have a seminar; he is going to hold a study group.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not for a moment pretend that in the two minutes which remain prior to the adjournment at six o'clock I can hope to do justice to the remarks which have just entertained us and enlivened the proceedings of this house, let alone to the remarks which have preceded the stirring and memorable observations which have just issued in a torrent from the mouth of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
I think I shall content myself, in these few remaining seconds, by saying that the hon. member for Essex East was undoubtedly at his theatrical best today. The flights of imagination were simply superb. We have grown accustomed to expect these flights in the airy realms of fiction, but today the hon. member was undoubtedly at his incomparable best. It was a demonstration, indeed, of an hon. member preaching without a text.
It was a wandering exposition. The hon. member included some Liberal padding by reading from the Winnipeg Free Press and from speeches made by his colleagues. Subtracting that padding from his remarks, they seemed to come down to this-that the hon. member is a self-confessed imaginative citizen.
